scenes.narration: The with statement opens a file, and closes it for you when the block ends. Think of an automatic door. It closes behind you, even if you forget. Write with open, the name, as f, and a colon. The indented block can use f. When the block ends, even through an error, Python closes the file. Closing matters. Text that you write can stay in a buffer. It reaches the disk only when the file is closed.

code.source:

print(text.upper())

scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We write Hello, and read the file straight back. It shows empty quotes. The text was still waiting in a buffer, because we never closed the file. Use with, and the file is closed when the block ends, so the text reaches the disk. Then reading it back works.

props.fixedCode:
with open("out.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Hello")
print(repr(open("out.txt").read()))
props.why: Written text waits in a buffer until the file is closed or flushed, so reading before closing can show an empty file.

shorts.title: The with statement
shorts.hook: "The with statement opens a file, and closes it for you."
shorts.script: The with statement opens a file, and closes it for you. With open, the name, as f, and a colon. Everything indented below can use f. When the block ends, Python closes the file automatically. It is like an automatic door, that closes behind you. You never have to remember to call close yourself. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Files that close themselves.

shorts.title: Even when errors happen
shorts.hook: "Here is the hidden power of with."
shorts.script: Here is the hidden power of with. If an error happens inside the block, Python still closes the file on the way out. Without with, an error in the middle can skip your close line, and leave the file open. With with, the cleanup always happens. That makes your programs safer, and the code shorter at the same time. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Safe cleanup.

shorts.title: Why closing matters
shorts.hook: "When you write to a file, the text may wait in a buffer in memory."
shorts.script: When you write to a file, the text may wait in a buffer in memory. It reaches the disk when the file is closed. If you forget, another program, or even your own next line, may see an empty file. Closing is not just tidiness. It is how your data is really saved. With does it for you every time. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Buffers explained.

shorts.title: The empty read
shorts.script: A strange bug. You write Hello to a file, then read it straight back, and see empty quotes. The text was still waiting in the buffer, because you never closed the file. Use a with block for the writing. When the block ends, the file is closed, the data is saved, and the read finds your text. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Close before reading.

shorts.script: Why did the file love with? It never had to say goodbye. Your challenge. Use a with block to open notes dot txt, and read its first line. Print that line without the extra new line. You should see Baga. Then try printing every line in capital letters, with a loop, still inside the with block. Share your code below. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 53.
